function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually) to get the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflow in place.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents so you can paste them into the appropriate files.

> **NOTE** – I’m unable to actually clone the repo or push changes from here, but the commands below will do it for you locally.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file called `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use official Node.js LTS base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> * The repo is a simple Node.js app (most likely an Express server).  
> * `node:18-alpine` gives you a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci` installs only production dependencies, keeping the image lean.  
> * Adjust the `EXPOSE` and `CMD` lines if your app uses a different port or start script.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder called `k8s` in the repo root and add two files inside it.

#### 2.2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### 2.2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *Replace `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `docker.io/zelarhq`).*  
> *If you want a LoadBalancer or NodePort, change `type` accordingly.*

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Login to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a kubeconfig secret)
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
        with:
          manifests: |
            ./k8s/deployment.yaml
            ./k8s/service.yaml
          images: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or token  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – a base64‑encoded kubeconfig file that allows the workflow to talk to your cluster

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.  
> You should see the build, push, and deploy steps in the Actions tab of the repo.

---

### Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, you can verify:

1. **Docker image** – `docker pull <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest`  
2. **Kubernetes** – `kubectl get deployments,svc -n <namespace>` (replace `<namespace>` with the namespace you deployed to)

---

That’s it! If you hit any errors (e.g., missing secrets, wrong image names, etc.), the Actions logs will give you detailed feedback. Happy deploying!
